newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia to revise forest industry policy.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia to revise forest industry policy.

text.p: British Columbia Premier Glen Clark said Friday he will soon announce policy changes to make forest companies more competitive and an accord aimed at increasing employment in the forestry sector.
"There will be some big changes coming. They will be controversial. There's no doubt in my mind about it," Clark told a forest industry group.
The changes would seek to help the industry be more profitable and increase employment.
Specifically Clark said "in the course of the next few weeks" the provincial government would be making changes in the Forest Practices Code that governs logging.
He said there would be no weakening of environmental standards but an attempt to make application of the controversial code more efficient and effective.
In addition, he said that "in the next few weeks...we will be, I believe, consummating a deal that I call the jobs and timber accord."
Clark has set a target of increasing employment in the forestry sector by 21,000 jobs over the next few years.
The government and forest companies have been negotiating for months on the issue and the industry has sought regulatory relief in exchange for a commitment to increase employment.
In addition, Clark said changes would be forthcoming in the coming weeks or months for the system under which stumpage fees are calculated on timber harvests.
This would primarily be aimed at the pulp industry where logs are "overvalued" under the current system, he said.

But, speaking to reporters after his speech, Clark said British Columbia would not make wholesale changes to stumpage because this would "invite retaliation from the United States." British Columbia does not want to undermine a Canada-U.S. lumber trade agreement, Clark said.
Another change to stumpage might include shortening the lag time between when changes in market prices are reflected in stumpage calculations.

The premier assured the industry that the government would not take money from the Forest Renewal fund to pay down its budget deficit. The idea was floated last year and roundly criticized. The fund was established in 1995 to revitalize the forest sector and forest-dependent communities and is funded by an increase in stumpage fees.
